title: Prefill scan and batch anomalies — sprint summary (2026-08-31)
content:
Purpose:
Notes from the sprint-long investigation into a recurring mid-sprint tail-latency regression that surfaced when prefill-scan sampling interacted with the coalescer/batcher. This document captures observations, short experiments, hypotheses, and the immediate mitigations we pushed. Aims: be concise for on-call handoff and to seed a follow-up RFC for longer-term fixes.

Meeting snapshot (2026-08-31 sprint retro):
Attendees: Aisha, Jonas, Mei-Ling, Connor, Priya, oncall rotation (Elliot for nightshift)
Overall tone: focused, pragmatic, hands-on

What happened (summary):
- Starting Aug 24 we saw intermittent p99 spikes on the hosted fleet (seq len 256–512 chat workload). Baseline p99: ~120ms for that class; spikes up to ~310ms.
- Symptoms: tail latency spikes correlated with increased number of microbatches of size 1 immediately following a prefill-scan pass. Throughput dropped 6–10% during spike windows. GPU utilization fell ~5% while CPU and host-side queueing rose.
- Observed primarily on model family A (v2.3 quantized) on dedicated nodes, but reproducible under a synthetic streaming load locally.

Key traces and signals we used:
- Trace: prefill-20260831-01 — shows repeated small-prefetch reads that preemptively touch KV entries then return no additional tokens, leaving coalescer to flush small batches.
- Flamegraphs: host-side scheduling hotspots in the coalescer's merge path.
- KD cache hit heatmaps: warmup pattern shows prefill evictions that collided with recent entries.

Initial hypotheses we considered:
1) Prefill-scan window too tight: scan logic aggressively prefetches KV entries in a narrow time-slice which causes many small, early wakeups to the coalescer.
2) Sampling bias: the prefill sampler preferentially picks requests with short-latency tails; when combined with packetized arrivals, it fragments batches.
3) Kernel scheduling race: kernel handshake and queueing priority can cause tiny batches to be dispatched with higher latency due to head-of-line stalls.
4) Shadow-cache eviction interplay: prefetch writes increase eviction churn and cause later requests to miss and re-prefill.

Experiments run during the sprint (what we tried):
A. Disable prefill-scan on a small canary pool (10 nodes) for 12h — result: p99 stabilized to baseline, throughput recovered. Confirms prefill is implicated, but not causal proof.
B. Increase prefill lookahead window from 50ms -> 200ms (staged rollout) — result: reduced microbatches by ~40%, p99 improved but tail occasional spikes persisted during ingress bursts.
C. Add jitter to sampler (stochastic 0–30ms) — result: reduced synchronicity; p99 improved modestly.
D. Tighten coalescer merge threshold to prefer waiting up to 10ms before flushing a single-request batch — result: microbatch count fell, but increased median latency by ~6ms (acceptable trade for p99).
E. Small kernel-priority patch (PR 2487) to prefer coalescer-merged dispatch when multiple kernels are pending — result: preliminary reduction in head-of-line stalls in synthetic load.

Root cause (working conclusion):
An emergent interaction between prefill-scan's eager touch semantics and the coalescer's flush policy produced synchronized wakeups that increased the fraction of size-1 microbatches. Those microbatches disproportionately penalized p99 because they created dispatch inefficiencies and prevented larger, more efficient batches from forming. Additionally, prefill activity increased short-lived KV churn that created transient misses for closely-following requests, amplifying the effect.

Immediate mitigations applied (production):
- Rolled back prefill-scan on the hot path for the affected model family for 36h while we validated fixes (canary group). (Owner: Mei-Ling, done 2026-08-26)
- Rolled out coalescer merge-threshold tweak across dedicated nodes (Owner: Jonas)
- Applied PR 2487 to reduce kernel dispatch races (Owner: Connor)
- Enabled sampler jitter by default for sampling-based prefetch (Owner: Priya).

Metrics after mitigations (first 48h):
- p99 returned to ~130ms average for the affected class (still slightly above historical baseline).
- Microbatch frequency (size=1) dropped by ~62% during peak ingress windows.
- GPU utilization returned to prior baseline; host CPU load normalized.

Open action items / follow-ups (priority ordered):
1) RFC: Prefetch design review — propose replacing eager scan with incremental asynchronous prefetch that signals the coalescer only when a minimum set of keys is available (Owner: Aisha, due 2026-09-10).
2) Experiment: deterministic prefetch backoff strategy (exponential backoff for repeated misses) — reproducibility tests in perf-lab (Owner: Mei-Ling, due 2026-09-03).
3) Long-term: integrate prefetch heuristics with the coalescer's queueing policy (shared signals so prefetch doesn't cause flushes) — spike design doc (Owner: Jonas, due 2026-09-17).
4) Add synthetic load test that reproduces arrival synchronization (senders with correlated inter-arrival) to nightly regression harness (Owner: Connor, due 2026-09-05).
5) Postmortem: write up incident note for oncall handbook and add quick mitigations checklist (Owner: Priya, due 2026-09-02).

Notes for SRE/Oncall:
- If p99 rises >2x baseline for more than 30m, consider disabling prefill-scan on the affected node pool and trigger an immediate rollback of recent coalescer changes only if rollback reduces microbatch frequency; otherwise contact eng-serving-runtime leads.
- Quick diagnostics: run the supplied trace filter (trace:prefill-YYYYMMDD) and check microbatch-size histogram (host.metrics.batch.size).

Lessons learned (retrospective):
- Eager subsystems (prefetch/prefill) should be treated as first-class citizens in scheduling design — they must expose flow-control signals to avoid accidental amplification.
- Small changes to timing (50ms vs 200ms) can change emergent behavior in non-linear ways; invest more in lightweight synthetic tests that model correlated arrivals.
- Jitter is cheap and effective as a short-term safety valve.

Appendix: quick repro recipe (perf-lab)
1) Start local coalescer instance with default flags, model A v2.3 quantized.
2) Run workload generator with 200 concurrent clients, seq len 256–512, peppered with a 1s burst every 30s to simulate interactive chat fanouts.
3) Toggle prefill-scan flag and observe microbatch histograms over 10-minute windows.
4) Baseline workload scripts and plot scripts are in: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serve/bench/synthetic-prefill

Sign-off and next sync:
- We'll reconvene in the next runtime sync (2026-09-07) to review RFC drafts and the perf-lab reproducibility reports.
- If anyone on the thread wants raw traces, ping me and I'll drop an aggregate link.

-- Aisha (prefill owner, eng-serving-runtime)
